title: Apply blush to both cheeks of a practice head, inside the drawn oval
instruction: Apply blush to both cheeks: sweep each brush over the inked oval on its cheek until it is covered.
context: Applying blush is a routine step in everyday makeup application; a 2016 YouGov poll found 38% of US women wear makeup at least a few times a week (26% never) (yougov.com/en-us/articles/48130-why-american-women-wear-makeup-poll).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left); heights above the table top. Practice head: vinyl cosmetology practice head, skull 19 cm front to back, 14 cm across, chin 12.5 cm and crown 31 cm above the table (as the accepted task 'put-reading-glasses-on-a-care-manikin'; cheekbone/jaw widths after Zhuang and Bradtmiller 2005), centred at (34.5, 0.0), facing the robot, fixed on its stand, taped to the table. On each cheek (centre 4.6 cm off the midline, 4.2 cm above the chin, 16.7 cm above the table): an oval drawn in solid ink, 4.4 x 2.8 cm, and a limit drawn in dashed ink round it, 6.8 x 4.8 cm. Right/left blush pan: round tin pan, 36 mm across and 3.94 mm tall (TKB Trading 36 mm pan), filled level with pressed (not loose) matte powder blush in one rose-pink shade from a single production lot, which swatches at about sRGB (215, 60, 105) on white paper (replace a pan when its swatch differs by more than 10 in any channel), centred at (30.0, -24.0) / (30.0, 24.0), held upright facing the arm in a small stand (a plain rectangular plastic riser, 30 x 15 x 23 mm, fixed to the table immediately behind the pan). Right/left blush brush: round blush brush, 157 mm long, 121 mm handle, 12 mm ferrule, 12 g (Kent TWMU10-style), clean, lying on the table bristles towards the head at (20.0, -17.0) / (20.0, 17.0). Rig protection: a 70 x 40 cm wipe-clean plastic drop sheet (2 mm thick, taped to the table) lies under the head stand, both pans and both brushes, and the head is wiped between trials, so loose powder does not reach the robot, its cameras or the table.
scoring: Tools: a phone camera, a printed 1 cm grid on a clear sheet, a 2 cm block. Covered: in a photo taken square-on to each cheek with the grid laid over it, the fraction of the drawn oval's squares showing pigment (under 40% scores 0 for that cheek, 40-80% scores 0.5, 80% or more scores 1.0). Bled: in the same photos, grid squares outside the dashed limit that show pigment, more than 1 square in all (about 1 cm2, the size of a shirt button) scores 0 for the whole run. Clear: judged from the trial video. A 2 cm block stands beside each cheek in view, and both brushes' bristles are at least that far from the skin for the last 1 second of the run; if not, the run is capped at 0.75. Pigment only appears where a loaded brush was pressed on the skin, and a brush only loads where it was pressed on its pan. The run's score is the mean of the two cheeks' scores, subject to the bleed and clear rules.
reset_notes: Wipe both cheeks clean, redraw the oval and limit in the same places, refresh each pan's cake surface level with the rim and check its swatch against the shade in the setup, wipe both brushes clean and lay them back beside their pans. Wipe or replace the drop sheet and wipe the head stand and the robot's fingertips with a damp cloth after each trial.
fidelity: The head, stand and pans are fixed rigid bodies; each brush is a free rigid body (bristle cluster collided as a convex hull). Pigment is modelled, not simulated: a brush loads from the cake only while its bristles press the pan with at least 0.3 N, and deposits on skin within 2 mm of the bristles only while they press the head with at least 0.2 N (PhysX contact force, smoothed over 0.1 s). No contact, or a lighter press, gives no pigment. No bristle deformation.
scores: demo: 1.0 (91% and 96% of the two ovals covered, no pigment outside the limits, brushes clear; scores 1.0 by 28.2 s / 564 steps); Dream-1 run: 0.0 (1,200 steps; neither brush was lifted from the table, so nothing reached the pan or a cheek)
